title: Load the CSV
summary: Read comma-separated data from standard input with the csv module.

steps.title: The project
body: Over four stages you will build a small data-crunching tool: it reads a sales CSV from standard input, cleans it, aggregates it, and prints an aligned report. It is the shape of a thousand real scripts, and in C# you would reach for a CSV library and LINQ. In Python the standard library and comprehensions are enough.
The tests pipe different files into your program, messy ones included.

steps.explain: Splitting on commas cuts the quoted city in two. `csv.reader` understands the quotes.

steps.title: Why the csv module
body: As you just saw, `line.split(",")` breaks when a field contains a comma. The `csv` module handles quoting:
text = sys.stdin.read()                 # all of standard input at once
reader = csv.reader(text.splitlines())  # any iterable of lines works
for row in reader:                      # each row: a list of strings
`csv.DictReader` gives dicts keyed by the header instead. Every value is a **string**; converting is your job in stage 2.

steps.prompt: Why read with `sys.stdin.read()` instead of `input()` in a loop?
options: It reads everything at once and never raises at the end of the input
It is the only way to read numbers
steps.explain: `input()` raises `EOFError` when the data runs out, and you do not know the row count in advance. `sys.stdin.read()` returns the whole input as one string.

steps.title: Load and count
prompt: Write `read_rows(text)` returning `(header, rows)`: the header as a list of names (stripped of spaces), and the data rows as lists of strings, **skipping blank lines** (rows where every cell is empty or whitespace).
Then `main()` reads all of standard input and prints:
Loaded 7 rows, 5 columns: date, region, product, units, price
Use `csv.reader`, since some fields are quoted and contain commas.
steps.starter:
import csv
import sys


def read_rows(text):
    ...


def main():
    ...


main()
solution: return header, [row for row in reader if any(cell.strip() for cell in row)]

tests.name: January file
tests.expect: Loaded 7 rows, 5 columns: date, region, product, units, price

tests.name: February file
tests.expect: Loaded 6 rows, 5 columns: date, region, product, units, price

tests.name: quoted fields
tests.expect: Loaded 3 rows, 5 columns: date, region, product, units, price

tests.name: header only
tests.expect: Loaded 0 rows, 5 columns: date, region, product, units, price

hints: `next(reader)` takes the header off the reader.
`any(cell.strip() for cell in row)` is false for blank rows.
